concepts.title: Spatiotemporal Filtering

position.section_title: Does the Human Visual System Use Matching to Estimate Motion?

concepts.one_liner: Spatiotemporal filtering uses the responses of velocity-tuned filters to estimate motion in image sequences.
concepts.content: Spatiotemporal filtering is a class of motion algorithms based on the principles of filter banks. These algorithms use the responses of velocity-tuned filters to estimate motion, often serving as an alternative to methods based on image correlations.
concepts.motivation_md: While many motion algorithms rely on simple image correlations, spatiotemporal filtering provides a principled way to estimate velocity by treating a video sequence as a 3D volume and applying filters tuned to specific orientations in space-time.

concepts.title: Fluted Square-Wave Motion Illusion

position.section_title: Does the Human Visual System Use Matching to Estimate Motion?

concepts.one_liner: The fluted square-wave motion illusion demonstrates how the visual system's reliance on low-frequency spatiotemporal energy can lead to perceived motion opposite to actual pattern shifts.
concepts.content:
Adelson and Bergen proposed a motion illusion that distinguishes between classes of motion algorithms used by the visual system. The illusion involves temporal filtering, motion processing, and aliasing. (see figure: Space-time signals, building toward the fluted square-wave motion illusion. The first row shows a stationary sine wave. (a) Movie of a motionless sine wave. (b) Space-time plot shows only vertical structure. (c) Spatiotemporal Fourier transform shows all energy on the zero temporal frequency axis because nothing is moving. (d) The second row shows a moving sine wave. (e) In the space-time plot, speed corresponds to local orientation. (f) The Fourier transform energy is sheared according to the sine wave’s speed. (g–i) The third row shows a moving square wave. The additional harmonics required to form a square wave are visible in (i) the spatiotemporal Fourier transform.)

The spatiotemporal Fourier transform of a stationary sinusoid $f(x,y,t) = \cos(\pi \omega x)$ consists of impulses along the $w_t = 0$ line, indicating no motion. A moving sinusoid has energy along a line perpendicular to the moving structures in the spatiotemporal signal. A moving square wave adds extra harmonics to this structure. If a square wave moves in 1/4 period jumps, its spectrum is replicated over temporal frequencies and multiplied by a sinc function. (see figure: Derivation of the fluted square-wave motion illusion, continued from @fig-motionIllusion1 . Top row shows that the square wave moves in 1/4 wavelength jumps, instead of continuously. This staggered...)

Because orientation in space-time indicates motion direction, velocity-tuned filters respond to the lowest spatiotemporal frequency impulses. If the lowest spatial frequency sinusoid is removed, the dominant orientation of the remaining lowest frequency components points in the opposite direction. While a pattern-matching algorithm would see the signal moving left, the human visual system—examining the orientation of the lowest spatiotemporal frequency components—perceives the signal moving to the right. This supports spatiotemporal energy models for human motion processing.
concepts.motivation_md: This illusion helps researchers determine whether the human visual system uses feature-matching (correlation) or spatiotemporal energy (filtering) to perceive motion, by creating a scenario where the two methods predict opposite directions.

  "- Removing the fundamental frequency from a jumping square wave can reverse the perceived motion direction.",
  "- The illusion supports the theory that human vision uses spatiotemporal energy filters rather than just pattern matching."
]

concepts.title: Pattern Matching Methods

position.section_title: Does the Human Visual System Use Matching to Estimate Motion?

concepts.one_liner: A class of algorithms used by visual systems for motion detection, typically based on image correlations.
concepts.content: Pattern matching methods are a class of algorithms that the visual system may use, often based on image correlations (see @Adelson85). These methods represent one approach to processing visual information, such as motion.
concepts.motivation_md: Pattern matching provides a way to understand how biological or artificial systems can identify motion or objects by comparing correlations between image regions.
concepts.recap_md: - Pattern matching methods are a category of algorithms used by visual systems for tasks like motion detection.

slots.motivation: Pattern matching provides a way to understand how biological or artificial systems can identify motion or objects by comparing correlations between image regions.

slots.example: Pattern matching methods are a class of algorithms that the visual system may use, often based on image correlations (see @Adelson85). These methods represent one approach to processing visual information, such as motion.

prereq.rationale: Understanding the illusion requires knowledge of how the visual system uses spatiotemporal filtering to process motion energy.

overlay.rationale: Spatiotemporal filtering is presented as a distinct alternative approach to correlation-based pattern matching for motion detection.
The illusion concretely demonstrates the visual system's reliance on spatiotemporal energy rather than simple pattern shifts.
The illusion is designed to distinguish between filtering-based and pattern-matching-based models of motion perception.
